unit.title: Perform weld in the flat and horizontal positions using manual metal arc welding process (MMAW)

summary: This unit teaches you to make sound fillet and butt welds in the flat and horizontal positions with manual metal arc welding (MMAW), building on basic stick welding. You will learn to set up and check the equipment, choose and store electrodes, prepare and fit single-V butt joints, make multi-run fillet welds (1F and 2F) and butt welds (1G and 2G) with the right angles and sequence, control distortion, and inspect your welds, name their faults and say how to prevent them.

blocks.p: This unit builds on basic **manual metal arc welding (MMAW)**, also called stick welding or shielded metal arc welding (SMAW). Here you go further: you make **multi-run fillet welds** and **single-V butt welds** in the **flat** and **horizontal** positions, on plate about 10 mm thick, to a standard that can be inspected and tested.

Most structural and fabrication welding in Jamaica is done in these two positions: beam seats, base plates, brackets, trailer frames, tank stands and machine bases are turned or set up so they can be welded flat or horizontal wherever possible, because these are the quickest and most reliable positions.
**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 2 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres who can already strike an arc and run beads with MMAW.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Work safely
Control shock, arc light, fumes, fire and burns; wear and check full PPE; protect others.
Set up the equipment
Check the machine, cables, holder and work clamp; set the polarity and the current for the electrode, joint, position and run.
Choose and look after electrodes
Read the classification, choose the type and size, and store and handle electrodes, especially low-hydrogen ones, correctly.
Prepare and fit joints
Bevel, clean, fit, gap, align, tack and pre-set plate for fillet and butt welds.
Weld fillet joints in 1F and 2F
Make single and multi-run fillet welds with the right work and travel angles and run sequence.
Weld butt joints in 1G and 2G
Make a root run with even penetration, then fill and cap runs, cleaning between runs.
Control distortion
Use tacking, clamping, pre-setting and welding sequence to keep the work straight.
Inspect and report
Inspect by eye and with gauges, name faults with their causes and prevention, and report results and problems.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on safety, equipment, electrodes, joint preparation, technique, positions, faults and inspection.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms and codes, such as SMAW, DCEP, 2F, root face) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Practical tasks**: a three-run fillet weld on a tee joint in the horizontal position (2F), and a single-V butt weld in the flat position (1G), both in 10 mm plate with 3.2 mm E6013 electrodes. The assessor watches your set-up, PPE, cleaning between runs and checking, not only the finished weld.

blocks.note: Learn the position codes (1F, 2F, 1G, 2G), the parts of the electrode classification and the names of the runs (root, fill, cap). Short-answer questions ask for them exactly.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.note: For a 3.2 mm electrode at about 100–125 A, American guide figures suggest **shade 10**; some European charts give 11 for the same current. Use your Centre's chart and your instructor's advice: if you cannot see the pool, the shade may be too dark; if your eyes ache or you see spots afterwards, it is too light.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: **Arc eye** is a burn to the surface of the eye from the arc's ultraviolet light reaching unprotected eyes. It feels like sand in the eyes, often hours later. People nearby can get it too.
**Synthetic clothing** (nylon, polyester) melts onto the skin when spatter lands on it. Wear cotton or wool, ideally flame-resistant.
Take lighters and matches out of your pockets before you weld.

blocks.note: In Jamaica's heat, gloves and shirts soak with sweat quickly, and sweat lets current through the skin. Keep spare dry gloves, change them when they get damp, stand on a dry board on wet or steel floors, and drink water and rest out of the heat so tiredness does not lead to mistakes.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: A cable with damaged insulation is repaired properly or replaced before use, never wrapped with tape and used. Report any fault, tag the equipment out of use and do not use it until it is repaired.

blocks.note: The electrode packet gives the current and polarity: "AC or DC+" means the electrode runs on AC, or on DC with the electrode positive. American books call DCEP "reverse polarity" and DCEN "straight polarity".
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Within an electrode's working range, **more current gives deeper penetration**, a wider, flatter bead and faster melting of the electrode. Set the current from the packet's range, then test on scrap of the same thickness and adjust in small steps.

head: Electrode size
E6013 (typical)
E7018 (typical)
rows: 2.5 mm
About 50–90 A
About 70–100 A
3.2 mm
About 90–130 A
About 100–140 A
4.0 mm
About 120–180 A
About 140–190 A

ul: **Root runs** use a smaller electrode or a current near the low end, so the root does not burn through.
**Fill and cap runs** use more current, so they fuse well into the side walls and the run below.
**Fillet welds** usually need a little more current than a bead on plate of the same thickness, because the heat flows into two plates.
**Horizontal welds (2F and 2G)** often run at the same current as flat welds or a little less, so the pool does not sag.
**Too high:** spatter, a red-hot electrode, undercut and burn-through. **Too low:** sticking, poor fusion, a tall, narrow bead and trapped slag.

blocks.note: These are typical ranges only. Every maker prints its range on the packet: use it, test on scrap, and follow your instructor.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: The **duty cycle** on the rating plate tells you how many minutes in every 10 the machine can weld at a current. Multi-run welds keep the machine busy: if the overheat light comes on, stop and let it cool as the maker says.

On DC, magnetism can push the arc to one side (**arc blow**), mostly near the ends of a joint. Move the work clamp, angle the electrode against the blow, weld towards a heavy tack, hold a shorter arc, or change to AC.

sections.title: Electrodes for flat and horizontal welding

blocks.p: Mild steel electrodes are often marked with the American (AWS) classification, such as **E6013** or **E7018**. Many packets also show an ISO code; your instructor will show you how to read it.

head: Part of the code
What it tells you
Examples
rows: E
Electrode, for arc welding
First two digits
Minimum tensile strength of the weld metal, in thousands of psi
60 = 60 000 psi (about 414 MPa); 70 = 70 000 psi (about 483 MPa)
Third digit
Positions: 1 = all positions; 2 = flat and horizontal fillets only; 4 = flat, horizontal, overhead and vertical-down
E6013 and E7018: all positions. E7024: flat and horizontal fillets only
Last two digits together
The type of flux coating and the current it runs on
13 = rutile, AC or DC; 18 = low hydrogen with iron powder, AC or DC+; 24 = rutile with iron powder, AC or DC

head: Electrode
Type
Used for
Points to know
rows: Rutile
General mild steel fabrication; the electrode for this unit's practical tasks
Easy to strike; smooth bead; easy slag
All positions; AC or DC
Low hydrogen (basic), with iron powder
Load-bearing and structural welds, thicker plate, crack-sensitive work
Stronger, crack-resistant weld metal
Must be kept very dry, in an oven
Hold a very short arc
Rutile with a lot of iron powder
Large, fast fillet welds in the flat and horizontal positions
Very high deposition; smooth, flat beads
Flat and horizontal fillets only
Cellulosic
Deep-penetrating root runs, pipe work
Forceful arc; more spatter
Never baked like E7018

blocks.p: The size of an electrode, such as **3.2 mm**, is the diameter of its **metal core wire**, not of the coating. Root runs in a single-V butt are often made with 2.5 mm or 3.2 mm electrodes, and fill and cap runs with 3.2 mm or 4.0 mm.
The **flux coating** burns to make a gas shield round the arc, forms a layer of **slag** that protects the hot weld and slows its cooling, steadies the arc, and cleans the weld metal.

ul: The flux coating soaks up moisture from the air. **Damp electrodes** cause porosity, spatter and an unsteady arc; with low-hydrogen electrodes the moisture puts hydrogen into the weld, which can cause **cracking**.
Keep rutile electrodes (E6013, E7024) sealed or in a closed, dry cabinet, off the floor and away from doors and windows. If they get damp, dry them only as the packet says.

Keep **E7018** sealed until needed. Once a packet is opened, keep the electrodes in a heated **holding oven** at the temperature the maker gives (often about 120–150 °C), and take out only what you will use soon, ideally in a heated portable quiver.

Low-hydrogen electrodes left out longer than the procedure allows (often about 4 hours in open air) go back to be re-dried exactly as the maker says (often about 350 °C for 1–2 hours), or are not used for the job.
Handle electrodes with clean, dry gloves; do not bend, drop or knock them.
Set aside any electrode whose coating is cracked, chipped, crumbling or damp. A damaged coating gives poor shielding.

blocks.note: Humid air and the rainy seasons make damp electrodes a daily problem in Jamaica. An opened box of E7018 left on a shelf by an open door can pick up enough moisture in a day to cause porosity and cracking. Put electrodes back in the oven or cabinet at every break.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ISO code
Weld

2F

blocks.p: The **3** codes (3F, 3G) are vertical and the **4** codes (4F, 4G) overhead: they are not part of this unit. In any position other than flat, **gravity pulls the pool downwards**; in 2F and 2G it tends to sag onto the lower plate, leaving undercut on the upper edge.

head: Preparation
Typical use
Typical sizes (follow the drawing or job sheet)
rows: Square edge
Thin plate, up to about 3 mm, welded from one side
Gap about 1–2 mm
Single-V
Plate from about 6 mm, welded from one side; the usual test joint in 10 mm plate
Each edge bevelled about 30°: about **60° included angle**
Root face (land) about 2–3 mm
Root gap about 2.5–3 mm
Single-V for 2G
Horizontal butt joints
Some procedures bevel only the upper plate, or bevel it more, so the lower plate forms a shelf that supports the pool; follow your job sheet
Single-V with a backing strip
Joints welded from one side where the back cannot be reached
A steel strip tacked under the joint; the root fuses into it, so a wider gap can be used

flow: Read the drawing: plate size and thickness, joint, weld size, position
Cut the plates and bevel each edge by grinding or flame cutting; grind the root face
Clean the bevels and about 25 mm each side, top and bottom, to bright metal: mill scale, rust, oil and paint cause porosity and poor fusion
Set the root gap with a spacer of the right thickness (a bare electrode wire is often used), and check that the plates are level and in line
Tack each end in the root, about 10–15 mm long, and check the gap again
Set a small **pre-set** angle (often a few degrees) so the shrinking weld pulls the plates flat
Chip the slag off the tacks and grind their ends to a taper so the root run blends in

blocks.note: On a long butt joint the gap tends to close up ahead of the weld as the root shrinks. Tack firmly, check the gap at the far end before you get there, and ask your instructor whether to set the finishing end slightly wider.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Clean both plates to bright metal where the weld and its toes will be.
Fit the upright plate tight to the base plate, with no gap at the root, and check it square with an engineer's square.
Tack each end (on the opposite side to the first run where the procedure allows) and check square again.

blocks.p: The weld and the metal beside it expand as they heat and **shrink** as they cool. Because the heating is uneven, the shrinkage pulls the work out of shape: a single-V butt joint bends up on the cap side, and a tee joint pulls its upright plate over towards the weld.

head: Method
How it helps
rows: Good tacks, clamps, jigs or strongbacks
Hold the parts in line while the welds cool
Pre-setting
Sets the parts slightly out the opposite way, so shrinkage pulls them straight
Balanced sequence
Welding opposite sides in turn, or back-step welding in short lengths, so the pulls cancel out
No more weld than needed
Every extra run adds heat and shrinkage: weld to the size on the drawing, not bigger
Natural cooling
Let welds cool in air; quenching in water does not stop shrinkage and can crack some steels

sections.title: Fillet welds in the 1F and 2F positions

head: Term
Meaning
rows: Root
The inside corner where the two plates meet; the weld must fuse into it
Leg length
The distance from the root to the toe on each plate; the usual way a fillet's size is given
Throat
The distance from the root to the face through the middle; about 0.7 × the leg length on a flat-faced fillet with equal legs
Toe
Where the weld face meets the plate
Profile
The shape of the face: flat or slightly convex is usual; very convex or concave faces are faults on most work

ul: Tilt the joint so the two plates make a **trough** and the weld lies level, like water in a gutter.
Point the electrode straight down the middle of the trough, halfway between the two plates, with a **drag angle of about 10–20°** in the direction of travel.
Gravity holds the pool in place, so larger runs can be laid and a slight weave can be used: a single run of about 10 mm leg is possible.
Whenever a job can be turned so a fillet is welded flat, it is usually quicker and easier to make it sound.
Point the electrode at about **45° between the plates**, aimed a little more at the **bottom plate**, with a drag angle of about 10–20°.
Hold a **short arc** and travel steadily, watching both toes.

Gravity pulls the pool onto the bottom plate. If the arc is aimed too high, or held too long, it melts a groove (**undercut**) along the upper toe; if travel is too slow, or the run is too big, the metal rolls over onto the bottom plate (**overlap**).
A single run in 2F is usually limited to about **8 mm leg**. Bigger fillets are made in several runs.

head: Run
Where it goes
Electrode angle
rows: 1: root run
Into the root, fusing both plates
About 45° between the plates; drag about 10–20°
Along the bottom plate, overlapping about half of the root run
Angled more towards the bottom plate; same drag angle
Along the top, overlapping about half of run 2 and fusing into the upright plate
Angled slightly up towards the upright plate, so the metal does not sag and the upper toe is filled

ul: **Chip and wire-brush off all the slag** after every run, and check the run before you lay the next. Slag left on is trapped under the next run as a slag inclusion.
**Stagger the stops and starts** of each run, so they do not line up across the weld. A weak spot at a restart is then backed by sound weld in the other runs.
Fill the crater at the end of every run: pause, or move back a little, before lifting the arc away.
Larger fillets are built the same way in more layers: for example three layers of one, two and three runs.

blocks.note: At the end, check that both legs are **equal** and to the size on the drawing with a fillet gauge, the face is flat or slightly convex, and the upper toe has no undercut. A fillet much bigger than drawn is also a fault: it wastes electrodes and time and adds distortion.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Butt welds in the 1G and 2G positions

blocks.p: A single-V butt weld in 10 mm plate is made in several **runs**: a **root run** that fuses right through to the back of the joint, **fill runs** that fill the groove, and a **cap run** (capping run) that finishes the face.

ul: Use a 2.5 mm or 3.2 mm electrode, with the current towards the low end of its range.
Point the electrode straight down into the joint (square to the plate from the side), with a drag angle of about 10–20°.
Hold a short arc and keep a small **keyhole**, a hole at the front of the pool that melts both root faces. Keep it the same size all the way along.
If the keyhole grows, speed up a little or lower the angle; if it closes and the arc sits on top, slow down a little or ask about the current.
Look at the back afterwards: there should be an even **penetration bead**, usually about 1–2 mm high, along the whole joint, with no gaps and no drips.

blocks.p: Chip and brush off every bit of slag. The root run often has a hump in the middle and slag lines trapped at its edges: **grind** them out, so the first fill run can fuse cleanly into the side walls.

ul: Fill the groove with stringer beads or a slight weave, fusing each run into both side walls and the run below. Clean after every run.
Leave the last fill run about 1–1.5 mm below the plate surface, with the bevel edges still showing, as a guide for the cap.

Lay the cap with a weave (or overlapping stringers on a wide joint), pausing at each edge so the toes are filled. It should cover each bevel edge by about 1–2 mm and stand a little above the plate, usually no more than about 3 mm, with even ripples.
Stagger the stops and starts of each run, and fill every crater.

blocks.p: In 2G the plates stand upright, one above the other, and the weld line runs horizontally. Gravity pulls the pool down onto the lower plate, so the technique changes.

ul: Use **stringer beads**, not a wide weave: a wide weave sags onto the lower plate and undercuts the upper one.
Make the root run with the electrode pointing slightly upwards into the joint and a drag angle of about 10–20°.
Build the fill and cap as **stacked stringer beads from the bottom up**, each overlapping the one below by about half.

Point the electrode slightly upwards for the beads along the lower plate, so they do not sag; for the top bead, hold it nearer level or point it slightly down, so it fuses into the upper plate without undercut.
Keep a short arc and a steady speed; the current is often a little lower than for 1G.

blocks.note: Welds made from both sides (for example a double-V joint) need the root of the first side **back-gouged or ground** from the second side until sound weld metal shows, before the second side is welded.
blocks.label: Tip

Likely causes

Travel too fast; gap too small or root face too big; current too low; arc too long
Burn-through or a large drip on the back

sections.title: Inspecting welds, faults and simple tests

head: Stage
What to check
rows: Before welding
Preparation and fit-up: bevel angle, root face, root gap, alignment, pre-set, cleanliness, dry electrodes, correct current and polarity
During welding
Each run cleaned and checked: no slag left, no cracks, good fusion, stops and starts staggered
After welding
The finished weld, cleaned of slag and spatter, by eye and with gauges

blocks.h: Visual inspection of a finished weld

ul: Let the weld cool, chip off all the slag and wire-brush it. Look along its whole length in good light, from both ends and the side.
**Fillet welds:** check the leg lengths with a **fillet gauge**, both legs equal and to size; check the throat if the drawing gives it.
**Butt welds:** check the cap's width and height (the reinforcement), and the penetration bead on the back.
Look for undercut, overlap, porosity, cracks, slag on the surface, unfilled craters, arc strikes and spatter.
Check that the plates are still square, in line and flat.
Record what you find and report anything that does not meet the standard.

blocks.p: The amount of each fault that is allowed (for example the depth of undercut, or the height of reinforcement) is set by the code, the drawing or your instructor. Cracks are never accepted.

blocks.note: Name the fault, give its likely cause and say what you will change. That is exactly what the assessor wants to hear about your own welds and other trainees' welds.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Test
How it is done
What it shows
rows: Fillet break test
The upright plate of a short fillet test piece is hammered or pressed over until the weld breaks open at its root
On the broken faces: whether the weld fused into the root and both plates, and any porosity or slag inside
Macro etch
A slice is cut across the weld, ground smooth and etched with a mild acid by the instructor
The shape of the weld, its penetration and fusion, and the runs
Bend test
A strip cut across a butt weld is bent round a former, with the face or the root on the outside
Whether the weld is sound and ductile: defects open up as cracks

blocks.p: Other tests, such as dye penetrant, magnetic particle, ultrasonic and radiographic testing, are carried out by trained and qualified inspectors.

sections.title: Finishing the job, housekeeping and reporting

flow: Finish the run and fill the crater
Take the stub out of the holder and put it in the metal stub container
Hang the holder on its insulated hook, clear of the work, the bench and the floor
Switch off at the machine, then at the supply
Coil the leads loosely and hang them up off the floor
Return unused electrodes to their packet, cabinet or oven
Leave hot work to cool in a safe place, marked HOT; move it with tongs
Sweep up slag, stubs and spatter, and check the area for anything smouldering

ul: Keep the booth clear: no offcuts, stubs or tools on the floor, and leads out of walkways.
Stubs stay hot and roll underfoot: always a **metal** container, never a paper or plastic bin.
Keep the floor dry and free of oil, and keep extinguishers, exits and the main switch clear.
Mark each test piece with your name, the position (for example 2F) and the date, so it can be inspected and tested.

head: What to report
Examples
rows: Damaged or faulty equipment
Cut cable, cracked holder, weak work clamp, a machine that trips, smells of burning or overheats often
Materials
Damp or damaged electrodes, a holding oven that is not hot, plate or electrodes running short
Injuries and near misses
Burns, arc eye, a tingle from the holder, a small fire put out
Your work
Welds finished, faults found and corrected, faults you could not correct, measurements taken

blocks.p: Damaged equipment is switched off, tagged DO NOT USE and reported, and not used until it has been repaired. Fill in the job card or logbook as your Centre requires.
Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise with your instructor.

ul: I can name the hazards of MMAW and the controls for each, and choose and check my PPE, including the filter shade.
I can check the machine, cables, holder and work clamp, and explain why each check matters.
I can set AC, DCEP or DCEN as the electrode packet says, and explain what each means.
I can set the current for the electrode size, joint, position and run, and explain how current affects the weld.
I can read an electrode classification, including what its third digit says about positions.
I can choose between E6013, E7018 and E7024 for a job, and store and handle low-hydrogen electrodes correctly.
I can name the positions 1F, 2F, 1G and 2G and describe how each joint is set.
I can prepare a single-V butt joint: bevel, root face, cleaning, root gap, alignment, tacks and pre-set.
I can explain what causes distortion and use tacking, clamping, pre-setting and sequence to control it.
I can weld single-run and three-run fillet welds in 2F, with the right angles and run order, and fillet welds in 1F.
I can make a root run with an even penetration bead, clean and grind it, and fill and cap a single-V butt weld in 1G.
I can make a butt weld in 2G with stacked stringer beads.
I can clean between runs and stagger stops and starts.
I can inspect a weld by eye and with a fillet gauge, and name faults with their causes and prevention.
I can describe a fillet break test, a macro etch and a bend test.
I can shut down, clean up and report faults, damage and injuries.

terms: 1F, 2F
Fillet weld in the flat position; fillet weld in the horizontal position
1G, 2G
Groove (butt) weld in the flat position; groove weld in the horizontal position
Back gouging
Removing the root of the first side of a weld from the second side, down to sound metal
Cap run
The final run, or runs, on the face of a butt weld; also called the capping run
DCEP
Direct current electrode positive: the electrode lead on the positive terminal
Distortion
Bending or pulling out of shape caused by the weld shrinking as it cools
Drag angle
The angle the electrode leans back from upright, towards the finished weld, as you travel
Fill run
A run that fills the groove of a butt weld between the root and the cap
Fillet gauge
A gauge for measuring the leg length or throat of a fillet weld
Included angle
The total angle between the two bevelled edges of a joint, for example 60°
Keyhole
The small hole at the front of the pool in a root run that shows the root is melting through
Leg length
The distance from the root to the toe of a fillet weld on each plate
Low-hydrogen electrode
An electrode such as E7018 whose coating must be kept very dry to avoid hydrogen cracking
Overlap
Weld metal lying on the plate at the toe without being fused to it
Penetration bead
The weld metal showing on the back of a root run
Porosity
Gas holes in the weld metal
Pre-set
Setting parts slightly out of line before welding so that shrinkage pulls them straight
Reinforcement
Weld metal standing above the plate surface on a butt weld
Root face
The small flat left at the bottom of a bevelled edge; also called the land
Root gap
The space between the plates at the root of a butt joint
Root run
The first run in a joint, which fuses the root
Slag
The layer of fused flux that covers a finished bead
Slag inclusion
Slag trapped inside the weld or between runs
SMAW
Shielded metal arc welding: another name for MMAW
Stringer bead
A run made without side-to-side movement
Tack weld
A short weld that holds the parts in place before the full weld is made
Throat
The distance from the root to the face of a fillet weld, through its middle
Undercut
A groove melted into the plate along the toe and left unfilled

c1.title: Bus-shelter brackets in Half Way Tree
c1.text: Kemoy is welding tee-joint brackets of 10 mm plate for new bus shelters in Half Way Tree, St Andrew. The brackets are welded in the horizontal position (2F) with 3.2 mm E6013 electrodes on a DC inverter; the packet gives 90–130 A, and he has set 115 A. The drawing asks for 10 mm fillet welds made in three runs. On his first bracket there is a groove along the toe on the upright plate.

c2.title: A trailer base plate in Port Antonio
c2.text: Petrina is butt welding two pieces of 10 mm plate in the flat position (1G) to make a base plate for a fishing-boat trailer in Port Antonio, Portland. The edges are bevelled at 30° with a 2 mm root face, and she sets a 3 mm root gap. She tacks the plates flat on the bench with no pre-set. On the root run she speeds up over the last third of the joint to catch up with her classmates.

c3.title: Horizontal butt practice in Falmouth
c3.text: At a training centre in Falmouth, Trelawny, Sheneil is practising single-V butt welds in the horizontal position (2G) on 10 mm plates clamped upright on a stand. She is using a wide side-to-side weave for her fill runs, as she did on flat welds. The fill keeps sagging onto the lower plate, and there is undercut along the upper plate.

c4.title: Beam seats for a hotel extension in Ocho Rios
c4.text: Romaine is welding steel beam seats for a hotel extension in Ocho Rios, St Ann. Each seat is a tee joint in 12 mm plate, and the engineer has specified E7018 electrodes. The shop's only machine is a transformer that gives AC, and the E7018 packet says "AC or DC+". The seats are small enough to be turned on the bench.

c5.title: Checking a test piece in Lucea
c5.text: At a training centre in Lucea, Hanover, Keisha is asked to inspect a classmate's 2F fillet test piece in 10 mm plate before it goes for a break test. The job sheet asks for 8 mm equal-leg fillets. She measures legs of 10 mm on the bottom plate and 6 mm on the upright plate, and finds an unfilled crater at the stop end.

questions.q: Why does the drawing ask for Kemoy's 10 mm fillets to be made in three runs instead of one?
o: Three runs use fewer electrodes than one large run
One run that big sags in 2F and fuses poorly
E6013 electrodes can only be used for small, single runs
Three runs put less total heat into the bracket
questions.why: In the horizontal position a single run is usually limited to about 8 mm leg; bigger, the pool sags onto the bottom plate and undercuts the upright. Several smaller runs give the size with a good shape and fusion.

questions.q: After the root run, where should Kemoy lay the second run?
o: Along the upright plate, lying on top of the root run
Straight over the root run, covering all of it evenly
Along the bottom plate, overlapping half the root run
On the other side of the tee, to balance the heat input
questions.why: The second run goes along the bottom plate, overlapping about half of the root run, and the third along the top, fusing into the upright plate. Building from the bottom lets each run support the next.

questions.q: Kemoy's current is inside the packet's range. What most likely caused the groove along the upright plate's toe?
o: Travelling too slowly along the joint
Using DC rather than AC for E6013
Too low a current for a 3.2 mm electrode
The arc aimed too high, or held too long
questions.why: With the current in range, undercut on the upper toe in 2F usually comes from aiming the arc too high on the upright plate or holding a long arc. Aim slightly more at the bottom plate and keep the arc short.

questions.q: On each bracket, Kemoy's electrode runs out at the same point in all three runs, so his restarts line up across the weld. Why is this a problem?
o: Restarts that line up use up more electrodes overall
Any weak spots at the restarts all fall together
The slag from each run cannot be chipped off
The weld will be too wide at that one point
questions.why: A restart is the most likely place for a small fault. Staggering the stops and starts means a weak spot in one run is backed by sound weld in the others.

questions.q: After welding, Petrina's base plate has bent up into a shallow V along the joint. What would have prevented this?
o: Cooling the finished weld quickly with water
Using a bigger electrode so there are fewer runs
Pre-setting the plates a few degrees the other way
Leaving out the tacks so the plates can move freely
questions.why: A single-V weld shrinks more on its wide cap side and bends the plates up towards it. Pre-setting them a few degrees the opposite way lets the shrinkage pull them flat; quenching does not stop shrinkage.

questions.q: On the back of the joint, the penetration bead disappears along the last third, where Petrina sped up. What has happened?
o: Incomplete root penetration: too fast to keep the keyhole
Excess penetration: the faster travel put in too much heat
Porosity: the faster travel let air into the root
Undercut: the faster travel melted the plate's top edges
questions.why: Travelling too fast closes the keyhole, so the arc sits on top and the root faces do not melt through. Keep the keyhole the same size all along by keeping a steady speed.

questions.q: Petrina's root run has a hump in the middle and thin lines of slag trapped along its edges. What should she do before the first fill run?
o: Weld straight over it with a higher current to melt the slag
Wire-brush the surface only, as the fill run will cover it
Grind out the hump and slag lines, then clean the joint
Lay the fill run with a wide weave to bridge over the slag
questions.why: Slag lines at the edges of a humped root run get trapped by the next run as slag inclusions and lack of fusion. Grinding them out gives the fill run clean side walls to fuse into.

questions.q: What should Petrina's finished cap look like?
o: Level with the plate, with the bevel edges still showing
Standing about 6–8 mm proud, so the joint is extra strong
Ground flush with the plate on both faces of the joint
Over each bevel edge by 1–2 mm, a little above the plate
questions.why: The cap fills the groove and overlaps each bevel edge by about 1–2 mm, standing a little above the plate (usually no more than about 3 mm) with even ripples. Too much reinforcement is a fault, not extra strength.

questions.q: What is the main change Sheneil should make to her fill runs?
o: Turn the current up so the pool freezes faster
Use stacked stringer beads, working from the bottom up
Keep the weave but make it wider so it covers both plates
Weld from the top plate downwards so the metal flows into place
questions.why: In 2G gravity pulls a wide weave down onto the lower plate and undercuts the upper one. Stringer beads stacked from the bottom, each overlapping the one below, keep the pool small and supported.

questions.q: For the last bead along the upper plate, how should Sheneil angle the electrode?
o: Nearer level or slightly down, into the upper plate
Pointing well upwards, the same as for the lower beads
Flat along the joint, with no drag angle at all
Straight at the lower plate, to support the bead
questions.why: Beads along the lower plate are pointed slightly upwards so they do not sag. The top bead is held nearer level or slightly downwards so it fuses into the upper plate and fills the upper toe without undercut.

questions.q: In what order should Sheneil lay the beads of her cap?
o: From the top bead down, so each one rests on the next
From the middle outwards, alternating up and down
From the bottom up, each overlapping the one below
In one wide pass from the bottom plate to the top
questions.why: The cap, like the fill, is built from the bottom: each new bead is supported by the one below it. Starting at the top leaves the first bead with nothing to hold it up.

questions.q: Can Romaine use the AC transformer with these E7018 electrodes?
o: No: E7018 always needs DC electrode positive
Yes: "AC or DC+" means AC can be used
No: AC can only be used with E6013 electrodes
Yes, but only if he connects the leads the other way
questions.why: "AC or DC+" means the electrode runs on AC, or on DC with the electrode positive. Polarity only applies to DC; on AC it changes direction 100 times a second whichever way the leads go.

questions.q: The beam seats can be turned on the bench. Why is it worth tilting each tee to weld its fillets in the flat (1F) position?
o: The pool lies level, so equal-leg runs are easier
E7018 electrodes can only be used in the flat position
Fillets welded flat need no cleaning between runs
The flat position needs no filter shade in the helmet
questions.why: In a trough the pool is held level by gravity, so larger runs with equal legs and good toes are easier to make, with less risk of undercut and overlap. E7018 is an all-position electrode.

questions.q: The supervisor suggests E7024 to speed up the fillets on a later job. Which is true of E7024?
o: It can be used in all positions, like E7018
It is a low-hydrogen electrode, so it must be oven-stored
It is a cellulosic electrode for deep root runs
It is for flat and horizontal fillets only
questions.why: The third digit 2 means flat and horizontal fillets only. E7024's thick iron-powder coating gives fast, smooth fillets in those positions but cannot be controlled vertically or overhead.

questions.q: Romaine took a handful of E7018 from the holding oven at 7 a.m. At 1 p.m. some are still lying on the bench. What should he do with them?
o: Use them up first, since they were dry this morning
Wipe them with a dry rag, then carry on using them
Return them to be re-dried as the maker says
Lay them in the sun for an hour to dry out again
questions.why: Low-hydrogen electrodes start taking up moisture as soon as they leave the oven; procedures often allow about 4 hours in open air. After that they are re-dried exactly as the maker says, or not used on load-bearing work.

questions.q: What do Keisha's measurements of 10 mm and 6 mm legs show?
o: The fillet is acceptable, as the two legs average 8 mm
The weld sagged downwards; the upright leg is undersize
The upright plate was not square, so the legs cannot be measured
The fillet gauge is faulty and must be checked first
questions.why: Unequal legs in 2F usually mean the pool sagged onto the bottom plate or the arc was aimed too low. Each leg must meet the size on its own: a 6 mm leg is undersize, whatever the other is.

questions.q: Which test will show whether the classmate's weld fused into the root?
o: Tapping the weld with a hammer and listening
Measuring the throat with the fillet gauge
Looking along the weld face in good light
Breaking the fillet open at its root
questions.why: A fillet break test opens the weld at its root, so the broken faces show whether it fused into the root and both plates, and any hidden porosity or slag. The face alone cannot show the root.

questions.q: How should the classmate have avoided the unfilled crater at the stop end?
o: Pause, or move back a little, before lifting the arc
Snap the electrode away quickly at the end of the run
Turn the current up for the last few millimetres
Grind the end of the run flat before it cools
questions.why: Snapping away leaves a hollow crater that can crack. Pausing briefly, or moving back over the run, fills the crater before the arc is lifted.

questions.q: Lascelles is welding on DC, and near the end of each joint the arc wanders to one side and spatters. Which change is most likely to help?
o: Move the work clamp and weld towards a heavy tack
Turn the current up and hold a longer arc
Change to a larger electrode at the same current
Leave the clamp where it is and weld faster
questions.why: This is arc blow, caused by magnetism on DC, mostly at the ends of joints. Moving the work clamp, welding towards a heavy tack, angling against the blow, a shorter arc or changing to AC all help.

questions.q: A fillet weld with equal 10 mm legs and a flat face has a throat of about how much?
o: 5 mm
10 mm
14 mm
7 mm
questions.why: On a flat-faced fillet with equal legs, the throat is about 0.7 × the leg length: 0.7 × 10 = 7 mm. The throat is always shorter than the leg.
